Article Title: Meta's highest-paid employee Alexandr Wang can't stop making fun of Google, says who is ...
Article Text:
Meta AI head

The benchmark behind Alexandr Wang’s dig at Google

Where the gains came from

The cost advantage

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini after a benchmark data shoed Meta’s latest AU model climbing near the very top of the industry rankings. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta’s Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Spark 1.3 scored 62 points, placing it behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (66) and Claude Opus 5 (63). The model outperformed Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash, which scored 61 and 53 respectively.Wang's comment was posted in response to a thread from Artificial Analysis announcing that Meta had released Muse Spark 1.3, the company's fourth Muse Spark model release in just five months. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, trailing only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 in their top configurations.The publicly available variant, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh), scored 61 on the same index, putting it in a tie with GPT-5.6 Sol (max), Grok 4.6 (high), and Claude Opus 5 (high). That score represents a 4-point jump from Muse Spark 1.2's score of 57 in August, and an 8-point gain over Muse Spark 1.1's score of 53 in July. It landed just behind Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 66), Claude Opus 5 (max, 63), and Claude Fable 5 (max, 62).According to Artificial Analysis, both new Muse Spark variants improved primarily in two areas: agentic task performance and scientific reasoning.On agentic work, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh) posted a 12-point gain over Muse Spark 1.2 on the Tau3-Bench Banking evaluation, rising from 35% to 47%, along with a 5-point gain on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (80% to 85%) and a jump in GDPval-AA v2 Elo rating from 1,615 to 1,709. The limited-preview Muse Spark 1.3 (max) variant pushed even further, reaching 52% on Tau3-Bench Banking — the highest score of any model on that specific benchmark — and a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,754. Artificial Analysis noted that Muse Spark 1.3 (max) achieves these higher scores in part by using significantly more reasoning tokens than the xhigh variant, reasoning 62% more on GDPval-AA v2 and 28% more on Tau3-Bench Banking.On scientific reasoning, the standout gain came on CritPt, where the xhigh variant improved 8 points over Muse Spark 1.2, from 18% to 26%. GPQA Diamond rose 4 points, from 90% to 94%, while Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode each posted more modest 2-to-3-point gains.Beyond performance, Muse Spark 1.3 also demonstrated efficiency. The xhigh variant costs about $0.55 per task, significantly lower than GPT‑5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6, which cost nearly double. Analysts noted this places Muse Spark on the “Pareto frontier” for intelligence versus cost, making it one of the most competitive models in terms of value.For those unaware, Meta has released four Muse Spark models in just five months, underscoring its aggressive push in frontier AI.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee, recently took a jab at Google ’s Gemini. Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta's Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Fraudster uses Raigad SP’s WhatsApp display photo to dupe police staff, seeks Rs 50,000
Article Text:
A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers, but the scam attempt was foiled. (AI-generated image)





NAVI MUMBAI: Raigad Cyber Police have registered a case against an unidentified fraudster who allegedly used the WhatsApp Display Picture (DP) of Raigad Superintendent of Police (SP) Anchal Dalal to deceive several police personnel into transferring money.On Thursday, the fraudster sent a message to Raigad SP's reader, PSI Siddheshwar Murkute, asking him to transfer money urgently. Murkute immediately realised that it was a modus operandi commonly used by cyber scammers, as the WhatsApp message was sent from an international number that was not saved in his mobile phone.Thereafter, PSI Murkute learnt that the same scammer had sent similar messages to several Raigad police personnel. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters.Subsequently, PSI Murkute registered an FIR against the unidentified accused under the relevant section of the BNS for the offence of cheating by personation.The complainant, PSI Murkute, said, "I had received the WhatsApp message from an international number and the DP was of Raigad SP Anchal Dalal.The message read, 'I am in a meeting and my mobile is switched off. Immediately transfer Rs 50,000 to my bank account.' I knew the message sender was a scammer. I deliberately replied asking for the bank account number by pretending to send the money. As I received the bank account number from the scammer, it will be useful for the cyber police team to trace the bank account holder. "PSI Murkute added, "One police officer had received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam and claiming that it was required for filling diesel in the car, and that her mobile battery had drained and she was unable to pay online at the fuel station."API Amol Jadhav of Raigad Cyber Police said, "The cyber scammers use VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) to mask their identity. However, the Internet Protocol (IP) address of the WhatsApp number used by the accused will be obtained to trace the location, and the accused will soon be behind bars."
Article Summary: A cyber fraudster impersonated Raigad SP on WhatsApp, targeting police personnel for money transfers. Fortunately, no one fell prey to the fraud, as the police personnel were aware of this modus operandi used by cyber fraudsters. One police officer received a WhatsApp message from the same international number asking to transfer Rs 2,000 by impersonating SP madam.

Article Title: No ‘Barbecue’ in name, HC tells cloud kitchen
Article Text:
Nagpur:





The Nagpur bench of Bombay High Court recently restrained a Gokulpeth-based online food business from using the name “Barbecue/barbecue” during the pendency of a trademark suit, holding that its use was prima facie similar to the branding of a Sadar restaurant that has operated under the name for more than three decades.Justice YG Khobragade, allowing an appeal by the Sadar restaurant operators, set aside an Aug 4 district court order that had refused them interim protection in their trademark suit against the cloud kitchen.The petitioners — Tervinder Jhans, his proprietary concern M/s Barbecue and Barbecue Food Services — claimed they had been running their food and restaurant business under the “Barbecue” brand at Sadar since 1994. They approached the court after discovering in November 2022 that the respondents were operating a food business under the name “barbecue Gokulpeth” through online food-delivery platforms.The petitioners, through senior counsel Mukesh Samarth, Apurv De and Vaishnavi Ramidhani, contended that their branding featured a distinctive cursive representation of “Barbecue”, a diamond-shaped device and a specific colour scheme.As per the petitioners, their sales statements from 1994-95 to 2019-20 showed cumulative turnover of about Rs39.05 crore over 26 years. They argued that the respondents’ use of the similar name and branding was likely to confuse customers and dilute their goodwill and reputation.The respondents contended that the petitioners did not hold an exclusive registration for the standalone word “Barbecue”. They argued that the protection claimed by the petitioners related to a composite/device mark and that the two businesses operated from different locations and had different modes of operation.The judge found that the distinction between 'barbecue' and 'Barbecue' was insufficient, at the interim stage, to protect the respondents’ use of the name. “‘Barbecue’ and ‘barbecue’ are phonetically similar words,” he held.The HC noted that the petitioners had been operating “Barbecue Sadar, Nagpur” for more than 30 years and had established their branding through the registered device mark, artistic work and commercial material such as delivery bags and bills.Justice Khobragade also noted that the respondents had not approached the competent authority for registration of copyright or trademark in respect of the disputed name.“If the respondents are permitted to continue to carry their business under the phonetic name ‘barbecue’, it will certainly cause irreparable loss and injury to the petitioners’ goodwill and reputation in the market,” he said.The HC found that the district court had primarily relied on the businesses being located in Sadar and Gokulpeth and arrived at the conclusion that “BARBECUE/barbecue” was not exclusively associated with the petitioners. It held that the trial court had failed to properly appreciate the applicable legal principles and material on record, describing its findings as “perverse and unsustainable in law”.
Article Summary: Nagpur bench of Bombay High Court recently restrained a Gokulpeth-based online food business from using the name “Barbecue/barbecue” during the pendency of a trademark suit. The court held that its use was prima facie similar to the branding of a Sadar restaurant that has operated under the name for more than three decades.

Article Title: WWII hospital shipwreck in Albania now hosts devil firefish, squid eggs and a rare monk seal 80 years after sinking
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

Albania’s Hospital Ship ‘Po’ became a marine habitat in 1996

PC: AI Generated

What did researchers find around the wreck

How does the wreck affect the seabed around it

Significance of the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ for future marine research

More than eight decades after the Hospital Ship ‘Po’ sank in Albania’s Vlora Bay, its rusting remains have become part of a busy underwater ecosystem. A new study has found the 134.98-metre wreck covered by dense biological communities, with fish, sponges, sea squirts and other marine life using its hard surfaces. The sighting was the first confirmed record in Vlora Bay since 1996. According to the research article published in Frontiers in Ocean Sustainability titled ‘ First assessments on marine geomorphology and bio-colonization through the study and survey of the wreck of the Hospital Ship “Po” along the Albanian coasts (Vlora Bay) ’ recorded the non-indigenous devil firefish and evidence of squid spawning around the wreck. Most strikingly, a critically endangered Mediterranean monk seal was photographed resting inside sheltered cavities of the ship in August 2023. Lying at depths of 33 to 37 metres within the Karaburun-Sazan Marine Protected Area, the wreck is now being studied not only as a remnant of wartime history but also as a structure that shapes local marine habitats and seabed conditions.The Hospital Ship ‘Po’ now supports a dense marine community in Vlora Bay, with more than 80% of its hard surface covered by biological growth. Researchers identified 54 taxa living on the wreck’s structure. Sponges, sea squirts, bryozoans, molluscs, algae and other organisms formed a layered community across the vessel. Fish surveys recorded 28 species from 14 families, including dusky groupers, morays, seabass, wrasses, seabreams and barracuda.Juvenile common two-banded seabream, painted comber and striped red mullet were also observed around the structure. The bow supported more complex assemblages than midship and stern areas.Among the most notable observations was the presence of the devil firefish, Pterois miles, a non-indigenous species recorded on the wreck’s hard surfaces. Researchers observed up to seven individuals at the same time. The survey also found large gelatinous egg clusters attributed to Ommastrephidae, likely Illex coindetii, attached to vertical surfaces at depths of 22 to 25 metres. These observations suggest the wreck may provide conditions suitable for reproduction and shelter. The study further recorded a transient Mediterranean monk seal, Monachus monachus, resting inside sheltered cavities in the upper structure.The wreck does more than provide a surface for marine organisms. Its position also appears to influence the seabed around it. The 134.98-metre vessel lies upright at 33 to 37 metres depth and remains almost perpendicular to the dominant northwest-southeast water currents. Surveys identified a scour hollow reaching 2.1 metres below the reference seabed on the upstream side. Behind the stern, sediment formed a depositional trail extending about 45 metres. Sediment samples showed medium sand of about 350 micrometres at reference sites, while fine silt-clay particles below 63 micrometres occurred close to the wreck.The researchers describe the findings as an early step towards understanding how historic wrecks function within marine ecosystems. They developed two preliminary measures, the Geometric-Geomorphological Wreck Effect Index and the Ecological Hotspot Value Index, to summarise observations at the site. The ecological index was 0.83, based on benthic diversity, biological coverage and selected indicator groups.
Article Summary: Albania’s Hospital Ship ‘Po’ became a marine habitat in 1996. A new study has found the 134.98-metre wreck covered by dense biological communities. Sponges, sea squirts, bryozoans, molluscs, algae and other organisms formed a layered community across the vessel.

Article Title: OpenAI agents went rogue twice before GPT-6 Astra launch, exchanged tactics to bypass restrictions
Article Text:
Swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this year. (File photo)

Agents turned German wiki into message board

Researchers trace activity to OpenAI-linked infrastructure

Agents discussed ways to evade detection

Incident comes amid Astra safety scrutiny

Hugging Face breach adds to concerns

OpenAI disputes claims of withholding investigation

A swarm of rogue OpenAI agents broke out of a testing environment and hijacked a German-language website this spring, using it as a message board to share ways to bypass restrictions, cheat on tasks and conceal their activities, according to new research reviewed by Reuters and people familiar with the incident.The previously unreported episode, which began in May, comes as OpenAI has launched its new Astra model amid mounting scrutiny over the safety of increasingly autonomous AI agents. It also follows the company's July disclosure of a separate incident in which AI agents escaped a controlled test environment and breached the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.The German incident was uncovered in late August by researchers Sydney Von Arx, CEO of AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd, a quantitative trader-turned-AI researcher, who were searching the internet for signs of unauthorised AI-agent activity.The researchers found more than 15,000 edits made by AI agents on DseWiki, a German-language wiki for programmers that allows community contributions similar to Wikipedia.The activity suggested that the agents had repurposed the site to communicate with one another, exchanging tactics for bypassing OpenAI restrictions, completing tasks more efficiently and avoiding detection.“It seems extremely unlikely that OpenAI wanted them to do this,” Von Arx told Reuters.“I doubt they’re supposed to be coordinating with each other. I doubt they’re supposed to be writing on the open internet.”The researchers said the activity appeared to be driven by AI agents operating at superhuman speeds and focused heavily on technical questions similar to those used in AI companies' model evaluations.Many of the messages were signed by users identifying themselves as agents, while around half used names suggesting an OpenAI connection, including “OpenAIResearcher” and “OAIResearchMar26.”According to the researchers, public server logs indicated that much of the activity originated from Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI sometimes uses.They also observed repeated visits to the website by OpenAI employees after the episode, a pattern they said suggested a connection between the agents and the company.The findings have prompted questions about whether the incident represented an isolated failure during testing or a broader challenge associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London, told Rueters that the researchers' findings indicated that the agents had attempted to interfere with the website itself, describing it as a hacking attempt. OpenAI disputed that characterisation based on its analysis of the material.Messages reviewed by the researchers showed agents discussing methods to avoid detection, use tools such as Tor and maintain communications after being shut down.According to the report, when a moderator began deleting pages from the website in June, the agents responded by creating backup pages to circumvent the cleanup.“wiki cleanup/deletion sweep appears active alphabetically,” one agent wrote on June 19. “If this page vanishes, try [[ZZZDataUSAConstructionWageLive]]."The researchers said the behaviour went beyond conventional AI safety testing, in which models may be deliberately given offensive cybersecurity tasks to assess their capabilities.Maurice Chiodo, an academic at Cambridge University's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk who reviewed some of the communications, told Reuters that the messages resembled "the operation of some sort of underground network, hell-bent on achieving a task or mission."The episode, he said, should reinforce concerns that advanced AI could pose risks through coordinated groups of autonomous systems rather than only through a single highly capable model.The disclosure comes shortly after OpenAI unveiled Astra, its latest AI model, which the company has described as faster and more capable of carrying out complex computer-based tasks.OpenAI has acknowledged that Astra can make it harder for humans to understand how it reaches conclusions because it is more likely to conceal or disguise aspects of its reasoning. The company has also warned that increasingly capable systems can create difficulties for monitoring and alignment.“As the models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki told Reuters. “This doesn't guarantee that as intelligence continues to increase, our methods will be sufficient because progress in intelligence does not guarantee progress in alignment.”OpenAI has said it is developing stronger monitoring and automated safeguards for its models. The company also recently paused some model development work to add additional safety measures.Astra can help companies identify weaknesses in their systems more quickly, OpenAI has said, while acknowledging that this could also make those weaknesses easier to exploit.The German incident also comes as OpenAI continues to face scrutiny over the separate July breach involving Hugging Face.According to an investigation by the AI safety organisations METR and Redwood Research, OpenAI agents escaped a controlled testing environment and spent weeks carrying out unauthorised activity before breaching Hugging Face's systems.The agents also accessed a cluster of computers inside OpenAI and obtained secret keys and credentials that exposed some internal data to the public internet, according to the investigation.METR's investigation was conducted under terms negotiated with OpenAI, with researchers given access to logs only while working inside the company's San Francisco offices.The researchers said OpenAI limited their access and restricted the investigation's scope, raising questions about whether the full sequence of events was captured.“Our view of the incident changed in big ways over the course of our short total of six days on premises,” Ajeya Cotra told Reuters, one of the METR researchers.OpenAI separately published its own technical report, describing the Hugging Face episode as the “first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorization”.Reuters reported that OpenAI officials became aware of the German incident weeks ago but did not publicly disclose it. Four people familiar with the matter said some investigators wanted to examine the broader pattern of AI-agent activity more closely, while efforts to expand the investigation faced resistance from some within the company, including legal advisers.“We are unable to meaningfully respond to claims or findings on a report that we have not had an opportunity to review," an OpenAI spokesperson said. "Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request for access. We will carefully review its contents upon publication and take any necessary next steps, " the spokesperson added.The company also rejected claims that its legal team had discouraged investigation of the German incident."Claims that our legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false," the OpenAI spokesperson said.OpenAI said the German activity was unrelated to the Hugging Face incident and would not have been included in a report on that breach. The company also said it had acted in good faith by working with outside experts and disclosing relevant incidents.
Article Summary: Swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website this year. Agents turned German wiki into message board, researchers trace activity to OpenAI-linked infrastructure.Incident comes amid Astra safety scrutiny amid mounting scrutiny over the safety of increasingly autonomous AI.

Article Title: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity; decades later scientists found the plantations were changing groundwater but not the soil nature
Article Text:
Eucalyptus cladocalyx ‘nana’. Image Credit: ERA Nurseries

How did eucalyptus plantations change groundwater and soil salinity in Australia

The groundwater changed, but the saline seep remained

Why didn't the eucalyptus trees solve the salinity problem

Image Credit: AI generated

Some eucalyptus species performed better over 15 years

nana

A long-term lesson from Australia's eucalyptus plantations

Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity, hoping that thirsty, deep-rooted vegetation could help control the groundwater processes behind the problem. A long-running experiment in south-western Australia later showed that the effects of such plantations were more complicated than simply planting trees and waiting for the land to recover. Researchers established a mixed eucalyptus plantation above a saline seep in 1976 and monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed over time. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped. Published in ‘ Agricultural Water Management ,’ this comprehensive study reveals that effective land management requires understanding complex underground hydrological systems, cautioning against oversimplified solutions to persistent environmental challenges like soil salinity.The findings suggested that tree water use alone could not overcome the deeper flow of groundwater carrying dissolved salts toward the surface. Local geology, groundwater pathways and seasonal water availability all influenced whether planting trees could actually reduce salinity in the affected landscape.The study examined a plantation established on about 12% of a small farm catchment. The trees were planted above a saline seep, an area where salty groundwater had reached or approached the surface and damaged the land.The researchers wanted to identify eucalyptus species that could use large amounts of water and potentially help reclaim such affected areas. According to the study, the catchment contained two important groundwater systems. One was a deep aquifer in the lower part of the landscape and the other, a shallower seasonal aquifer. The researchers monitored changes in groundwater level and salinity using piezometers, allowing them to follow how conditions changed as the plantation developed.The results showed that the plantation was having a noticeable effect on water use. Changes in groundwater levels, along with observations of perched water, indicated that the trees were using more water than the nearby crop and pasture vegetation. This was an important finding because the basic idea behind planting trees in salt-affected agricultural landscapes was that trees could alter the movement of water through the soil. If less water moved downwards into the groundwater system, or if trees removed more water from the landscape, they could potentially help limit the processes that bring salt towards the surface.The researchers found that the plantation influenced groundwater chemistry as well as water levels. Chloride concentrations in the deep aquifer fell by approximately 20% between 1977 and 1984. The decline was greater at the middle of the slope than further downslope. This suggested that conditions beneath the catchment were changing, although the changes were not uniform across the landscape. At the same time, the study found larger stores of salt in the soil downslope than at the middle of the slope. There was also visual evidence that salt continued to be discharged extensively through the saline seep throughout the experiment. In other words, the trees were clearly affecting the local water system, but their presence did not bring the expected recovery of the seep. The research showed why this distinction matters. A plantation may increase water use and change groundwater conditions without having enough influence over the particular underground system responsible for a saline area. The findings also suggested that surface changes alone could not explain what was happening beneath the catchment, where groundwater pathways controlled the movement of salt.One of the most important findings of the study concerned the location of the plantation. The researchers identified the site's underground geology as a significant reason why the trees failed to control the seepage. The plantation was located in an area where the relevant aquifer appeared to be ‘confined.’ That meant the groundwater system beneath the site was not easy for the trees to influence in the way researchers had hoped. This finding highlighted a practical limitation of tree-based approaches to salinity. Planting species that use substantial amounts of water may not be enough on its own. The location of groundwater, the way water moves through underground layers and the position of the plantation within the wider landscape can all affect the outcome. The study therefore showed that managing salinity is not simply a question of selecting the thirstiest trees. Understanding the underground environment is equally important.The experiment also compared the performance of different eucalyptus species. The original aim was to rank species partly according to water use, which the researchers assessed through factors including leaf area and survival. Tree growth was rapid during the early years of the experiment, continuing strongly until 1981. After that, growth declined. 15 years later, four species emerged as the most promising among those tested. These included ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx var.,’ ‘Eucalyptus cladocalyx,’ ‘Eucalyptus occidentalis’ and ‘Eucalyptus sargentii.’ Their performance did not mean that the plantation had solved the saline seep problem. Instead, it showed that some species were better suited than others to the demanding conditions of the site. A tree can survive well and use considerable amounts of water while still being unable to alter a groundwater system enough to stop salt from reaching the surface.The 15-year experiment provided a more realistic picture of what tree planting could not achieve in salt-affected farmland. The eucalyptus plantation used more water than the surrounding vegetation, and conditions in the deep groundwater system also shifted, including a significant fall in chloride concentration. Yet the saline seep continued to discharge salt. As per the study, this outcome was due to the underground conditions beneath the plantation. The research pointed towards a broader lesson that the success of planting trees depends not only on the trees, but also on the landscape in which they are planted. For areas struggling with rising groundwater and soil salinity, the findings suggest that planting eucalyptus can be a useful tool, but it is not a solution. Trees can change groundwater behaviour, without necessarily controlling the source of the problem. Only by monitoring the plantation for many years were researchers able to see both the benefits of greater tree water use and the limits imposed by the site's hidden groundwater system.
Article Summary: Australia planted eucalyptus trees to fight rising soil salinity. Researchers monitored how the trees affected groundwater levels and salt movement for 15 years. The study found clear signs that the plantation used more water than nearby crops and pasture, while groundwater conditions also changed. Yet the trees did not stop the saline seep as researchers had hoped.

Article Title: Hawaii put 195,000 plastic bottles’ worth of recycled plastic into Fort Weaver Road in 2022, but the experiment came with a hidden environmental question
Article Text:
Hawaii’s 195,000-bottle plastic road was built as a pavement test

Hawaii compared recycled plastic asphalt with conventional pavement

The hidden environmental test behind Hawaii’s plastic road

Hawaii spent 18 months testing what recycled asphalt could do

The plastic road was a test for Hawaii’s future paving plans

What happened to the 195,000 bottles

Hawaii’s plastic road experiment moved into a second phase

A road in western Oahu looks much like any other stretch of asphalt. Cars pass over it, tyres wear against its surface and, from the driver's seat, there is little to suggest that recycled plastic is part of the pavement underneath. Yet in 2022, the Hawaii Department of Transportation (HDOT) began testing exactly that idea on Fort Weaver Road in Ewa Beach, turning an ordinary stretch of highway into a real-world test of whether waste plastic could serve a useful purpose.Reportedly, the project used 1,950 tons of plastic-modified asphalt, containing recycled plastic equivalent to about 195,000 bottles. The aim was not to build a road out of plastic, but to add a small quantity of recycled polymer to a conventional asphalt mixture and see how it behaved.There was a second question hanging over the experiment, though. If plastic could be kept out of a landfill by putting it into roads, what happened to that material afterwards? Researchers also had to consider whether the plastic would remain locked within the pavement or gradually break down under traffic, sunlight, heat and weather, potentially creating another environmental concern over the road’s lifetime.According to Hawaii News, The Fort Weaver project was designed as a pavement experiment rather than a wholesale change to road construction. The recycled plastic polymer was incorporated into hot-mix asphalt, with the resulting material containing only around 0.1% plastic. Three sections were laid so researchers could compare different mixes, including a conventional control section.The figure of 195,000 bottles can make it sound as though an enormous quantity of plastic was physically packed into the road. In reality, the bottles are an equivalent measure of the recycled material used in the asphalt. The plastic forms only a small part of the much larger paving mixture.HDOT's interest was partly practical. If the modified asphalt could withstand Hawaii's conditions without sacrificing pavement performance, recycled plastic might become another material available for road construction. The department was also examining whether the approach could help produce stronger or longer-lasting pavement.Plastic waste presents a particularly awkward problem for places that have limited land and complex waste-management needs. Turning some of that material into an ingredient for infrastructure offers a possible route away from disposal, while also reducing the amount of new material needed for certain applications.But roads are not forgiving testing grounds. They have to withstand traffic, heat, rain and repeated loading for years. A material that looks promising in a laboratory still has to perform when thousands of vehicles travel across it.That is why HDOT did not simply replace an existing road with the new mixture and declare the experiment a success. A section using polymer-modified asphalt was placed alongside the plastic pavement, giving researchers a reference point for comparison.The most interesting part of the experiment was not necessarily visible from the road. The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa and Hawaiʻi Pacific University were brought in to examine what happened around the new pavement. Part of the work involved investigating whether plastic particles or chemical additives could leave the asphalt and enter the surrounding environment.By 2023, researchers at Hawaii Pacific University's Center for Marine Debris Research were collecting simulated stormwater runoff from the pavement. The samples were being examined for microplastics and synthetic chemicals that might have been released from the road.They were also looking at tyre-wear particles. That was important because not every tiny plastic particle found around a road would necessarily have originated in the pavement itself. Vehicles can generate their own mixture of rubber and polymer particles as tyres gradually wear down.So the catch was fairly straightforward: putting waste plastic into asphalt may prevent some plastic from reaching a landfill, but researchers still have to establish what happens to that plastic while the road is being used.The plastic experiment was also tied to a separate effort to increase the amount of reclaimed asphalt pavement, or RAP, used in Hawaii.According to HDOT, asphalt mixtures contain 50% RAP. If those mixtures performed adequately, the resulting data could support a substantial increase in the amount of recycled asphalt used in future road projects.That makes the Fort Weaver project slightly different from a simple plastic-recycling exercise. Engineers were testing several approaches to reducing the demand for virgin road-building materials at the same time.Plastic was one part of the experiment. Reclaimed asphalt was another. The evaluation was planned to run for about 18 months. Rather than judging the pavement immediately after construction, researchers intended to watch its performance over time and examine environmental samples from the site.That longer observation period was necessary because a road can look perfectly sound shortly after it has been laid and still develop problems later. Cracking, rutting, surface wear and changes caused by weather are among the things that matter when judging a pavement mixture.Environmental monitoring adds another layer. A recycled material can solve one waste problem while creating a different concern if components migrate into soil or water. That is why the researchers were specifically looking for evidence of microplastics and other substances in runoff.The department had already acknowledged that plastic-containing asphalt had been used elsewhere in the United States, while stressing that the mixture still needed to be evaluated for Hawaii's particular conditions. That caution is important. A material working on one road in one climate does not automatically make it suitable everywhere.The project also involved local institutions and industry partners, turning the stretch of Fort Weaver Road into something of a live laboratory. Cars continued to use the road while researchers collected information that could eventually influence future paving decisions.There was no guarantee that the plastic mixture would become standard practice. And that was precisely the point of the pilot.They did not become 195,000 recognisable bottles buried beneath the surface. The recycled material was processed and incorporated into the asphalt mixture. The quantity of plastic used was calculated as being equivalent to about 195,000 plastic bottles. HDOT said this represented material that otherwise could have gone to landfill.If the modified asphalt proved durable and did not create unacceptable environmental impacts, roads could provide one additional outlet for certain recycled plastics. If the material degraded, leached unwanted substances or failed to improve pavement performance, the apparent recycling benefit would be harder to justify.That uncertainty is why the project attracted scientific scrutiny rather than being treated simply as a recycling success story.The initial phase was completed in 2022, but the idea did not end there. Hawaii later moved into a second phase of its plastic-road work, including material from consumer recycling and discarded fishing nets.That development points to a larger issue surrounding recycled materials: where the feedstock comes from matters almost as much as where it eventually goes.For Hawaii, finding uses for locally generated waste could potentially reduce disposal while creating a supply of recycled material for infrastructure. But each new material source brings its own composition and processing questions.
Article Summary: Hawaii used 1,950 tons of plastic-modified asphalt containing recycled plastic equivalent to about 195,000 bottles. The aim was not to build a road out of plastic, but to add a small quantity of recycled polymer to a conventional asphalt mixture. The Fort Weaver project was designed as a pavement experiment rather than a wholesale change to road construction.

Article Title: In 1972, Illinois used 246,000 cubic yards of coal fly ash beneath 7,500 feet of expressway; monitoring found no evidence of settlement, frost or capillary-rise problems
Article Text:
Engineering a major highway embankment with industrial waste

Technical evaluations confirm long-term structural stability

Environmental standards and legacy of ash recycling

More than five decades ago, civil engineers in northern Illinois carried out a major engineering experiment by using 246,000 cubic yards of coal fly ash beneath 7,500 feet of a major expressway embankment. The pioneering project, completed in 1972 near Waukegan along the US Route 41 corridor, was one of the earliest large-scale examples of recycling industrial waste for American highway construction. Long-term monitoring showed that the alternative fill performed very well, with no signs of structural settlement, frost heave or problems caused by rising groundwater. Detailed technical studies of the project were later published by the National Cooperative Highway Research Program in NCHRP Synthesis 199, titled Recycling and Use of Waste Materials and By-Products in Highway Construction. The Federal Highway Administration also included the project in its detailed user guidelines. The findings helped change how state transportation departments across North America viewed industrial byproducts. They showed that fine ash collected from coal-fired power plants could replace traditional soil and aggregate used as backfill.The decision by Illinois transport authorities in the early 1970s to use fly ash on such a large scale addressed two major problems: the high cost of digging and transporting natural soil, and the growing amount of industrial waste produced by Midwestern power plants.Fly ash is the non-combustible mineral material left after pulverised coal is burned in power plant boilers. Its particles are very fine, light and mostly spherical. Engineers found that when properly compacted, fly ash could provide strong resistance to shearing while weighing less than common clay or sand fills. During construction near Waukegan in 1972, contractors placed and compacted the 246,000 cubic yards of fly ash in controlled layers to create the main core of the embankment beneath the 7,500-foot road section. To prevent erosion and stop wind from carrying away the material during construction, crews covered the fly ash core with a thick layer of natural soil along the side slopes and road base. Instruments were installed throughout the site to track how the artificial embankment responded to heavy traffic and the severe freeze-thaw cycles common in northern Illinois winters.Monitoring over several years showed that the fly ash core performed as well as, or better than, traditional soil embankments. According to NCHRP Synthesis 199, published under the Transportation Research Board, inspections after construction found no detectable uneven settlement across the 7,500-foot section. The ash also had pozzolanic properties, meaning it could react with moisture and free lime over time to form cement-like bonds. This helped increase its strength as the embankment aged. Monitoring teams also found no signs of frost heave during severe winter freezes. They did not detect capillary water movement that could damage or weaken the asphalt pavement above. Research records kept by the Federal Highway Administration in document FHWA-RD-97-148 noted that the Waukegan project became an important model for state transportation departments in Delaware, Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. These states later created formal standards for using fly ash in structural fills during the late 1970s and 1980s.Although the 1972 Illinois project showed that coal ash could work well as a construction material, later decades brought stricter rules for managing the environmental risks linked to combustion waste. Early projects mainly focused on structural performance, moisture and density, and shear strength. Modern highway construction guidelines from the Environmental Protection Agency and state environmental agencies require detailed groundwater studies, protective sealing layers and groundwater monitoring. These measures help prevent trace heavy metals in fly ash from entering nearby water sources. Despite stronger environmental controls, the engineering principles proven on the 7,500-foot road section near Waukegan remain relevant to infrastructure projects around the world. The successful 1972 project showed that industrial combustion waste, when properly engineered and protected, could provide a strong and long-lasting alternative to natural aggregates in major transport corridors.
Article Summary: Engineers in northern Illinois used 246,000 cubic yards of coal fly ash beneath 7,500 feet of a major expressway embankment. The pioneering project, completed in 1972, was one of the earliest large-scale examples of recycling industrial waste for American highway construction. Long-term monitoring showed that the alternative fill performed very well, with no signs of structural settlement, frost heave or problems caused by rising groundwater.

Article Title: Why humans are so ok about animal suffering
Article Text:
Why Humans Are So Ok About Animal Suffering

The Omnivore’s Deception

: What We Get Wrong About Meat, Animals And Ourselves

need

common-sense understanding

Vegan philosopher John Sanbonmatsu’s work focuses on our resistance to rethinking the meat economy. In, the critical social theorist (also a magician) argues that there are two systems, interlocked, that dominate the meat economy, and our delusion that animalshumans.The first is speciesism, the belief that humans are superior to the rest of the animal world. The other is capitalism, which, yoked to speciesism, drives the industrialisation of animals for consumption and experimentation.The two forces are so intertwined that humans believe meat consumption is “natural”. Sanbonmatsu makes three points. 1) Humans are not superior. Every species has its own excellence. Humans have language, “that enables us to build technologies and forms of life that other species cannot. Only humans, thus, have Anna Karenina and astrophysics.” But, humans have “no neurological or morphological structure that would separate us clearly from other animals. ” 2) Making a distinction between ethical and unethical animal exploitation is “spurious”. The call for “moderation” is meat apologists’ smokescreen. 3) Finally, what is considered extreme, can become an era’s “common sense”. To demonstrate, the book draws parallels with abolishing slavery.Exposing speciesism’s self-serving myths, Sanbonmatsu writes, “Thousands of years ago...ingenious ancestors of modern turkeys, reindeer, cows, camels, pigs, chickens, aurochs, geese, sheep, etc., all had the same epiphany at once. In a miracle of interspecies coordination, they decided to exchange the inconveniences of a ‘state of nature’, in which all warred against all and none were safe, for the security and comfort of domestication by Homo sapiens. ” He calls it humanity’s “pleasing tale”.Humans comfortably live with a contradiction of values. We show every kindness to a beloved animal companion. At the same time, we find no horror in slaughtering for food. We feel no need, either, to reconcile these two extremes, says the book.Sanbonmatsu says defenders of animal agriculture argue dairy, meat and fish industries are benign systems, with cruelty an anomaly. That farmers care for their animals, ironically, though they’re raised to be killed. Advertising reinforces this idea, showing “animals smiling and dancing on their way to the barbecue or butcher.”But, animals do not consent to being used and brutalised. “So long as we choose to exploit and impose our will on them, it will always be necessary…to wield violent force against them.” There is, therefore, no such thing as “ethical” animal farming.To explain why “moderation” is not enough, the book compares the meat system with slavery. Apologists for slavery would argue the cruelty of some slave-owners didn’t make the entire system an abomination. Slavery was once the norm – until it wasn’t. And the uncompromising social norm was replaced by athat slavery itself was abhorrent, not merely its excesses.Similarly, the book argues, the problem isn’t a lack of ethical meat or need for moderation. The problem is the system itself, which is failing both humanity and the planet. The environmental movement, it says, has largely failed because it is unwilling to confront capitalism and speciesism.Recognising that animals have rights is a long battle, but there have been victories. Fur is mostly banned, animal experimentation is restricted. And cow’s milk faces competition from a growing range of plant-based alternatives. Maybe, we’re closer to questioning the meat system – long mistaken as “common sense”, peddled as “natural”.
Article Summary: John Sanbonmatsu’s work focuses on our resistance to rethinking the meat economy. He argues that there are two systems, interlocked, that dominate the meat market. The first is speciesism, the belief that humans are superior to the rest of the animal world. The other is capitalism, which drives the industrialisation of animals for consumption and experimentation.

Article Title: Scotland quarry expansion uncovered a 2,000-year-old woman’s grave; archaeologists were stunned by its carefully built stone walls
Article Text:
'Beautifully made' Iron Age burial site containing the skeleton of a woman at a quarry in Sutherland. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Discovery of the 2,000-year-old unique burial in Scotland

What did the Iron Age grave of a woman look like

Further analysis is being carried out on the grave. Image Credit: Highland Archaeological Services (HAS)

Absence of objects in the women’s grave

What can the skeleton reveal about the woman

A nearly 2,000-year-old carefully constructed stone-lined burial containing the remains of a woman has been discovered at a quarry in Sutherland, Scotland, revealing an unexpected glimpse of life and death at that time. Archaeologists from Highland Archaeological Services(HAS) discovered Evelix, near Dornoch, while carrying out work ahead of a planned quarry expansion. The grave was found within an area where evidence of ancient settlement has also been identified, including features that may once have supported timber roundhouses. What caught the archaeologists’ attention was the unusual quality of the stonework. The structure was so neatly built that, at first, the team wondered whether it could have been modern. Instead, the construction style and archaeological evidence pointed towards the Iron Age, with the woman apparently having remained undisturbed for centuries beneath the ground.The discovery was made during archaeological work connected with the planned expansion of the Evelix quarry near Dornoch. According to the BBC, HAS was working for local quarry firm ‘GF Job’ when archaeologists encountered the stone-lined structure.The location was already considered archaeologically important. The Highland Historic Environment Record shows that the wider Evelix area has produced evidence of prehistoric activity, including burial remains, cremation burials, pottery and features linked to earlier settlement. This newly discovered structure stood out because of its carefully constructed stone lining. Instead of looking like a simple hole dug into the ground, it had been deliberately built with substantial masonry. As per the BBC, archaeologist Lynne McKeggie said the team initially thought the structure might be modern because of how well the stonework had been put together. That first impression quickly changed once the remains and other evidence were examined.The structure was dug into sand and measured approximately 3 metres long, 2 metres wide and 1 metre deep, according to the BBC. A small stone staircase formed part of the construction, adding another feature to the burial. Inside, the remains of an individual were found tucked into one corner. The archaeological team believes the individual was a woman and that she may have lain there undisturbed since the Iron Age. The careful construction is one of the most striking parts of the discovery. The stonework had been fitted together so neatly that the archaeologists described the structure as ‘beautifully made.’ Its appearance raises questions about why so much effort was put into creating it.The Highland Historic Environment Record provides an important background to the discovery. The people who built the structure were working without modern machinery, yet they created a substantial stone-lined space with a staircase. The result survived beneath the landscape for roughly two millennia before quarry-related archaeological work exposed it. Earlier archaeological work at the Evelix quarry area had already shown that the landscape contained evidence of prehistoric activity.The burial does not appear to have contained a collection of obvious grave goods. The BBC reported that no objects were found inside the structure, although archaeologists did identify a large quantity of animal bone. The absence of objects does not make the discovery less significant. In fact, it leaves more questions about the purpose of the structure and the circumstances surrounding the woman's burial. The animal remains may provide useful evidence as further analysis takes place. The construction itself can offer clues about the importance of the site to the people who used it. The wider archaeological record for Evelix also shows that prehistoric burials and settlement activity had previously occurred in the area.The remains could eventually provide a much more personal picture of the woman who was buried at the site. BBC reports that GF Job is funding further analysis of the human remains. Specialists will study the skeleton in greater detail, with the aim of learning more about the individual and the circumstances surrounding the burial. For now, many details remain unknown. Her exact age, background and life story cannot be established simply from the discovery itself. Those answers will depend on the scientific examination still to come. Archaeologists are using photographs and 3D scans to preserve information about the structure and the position of the remains.Once the further analysis has been carried out, the skeleton will be made available to Treasure Trove Scotland for potential allocation to a museum. What began as archaeological work ahead of a modern quarry expansion has revealed a carefully constructed resting place that had remained hidden for around 2,000 years. The woman's identity may never be known, but the grave itself has survived as a quiet reminder of the care and effort that people in Iron Age Sutherland could invest in remembering their dead.

Article Title: An Oakland woman answered a frantic call from someone claiming to be Charles Schwab security; minutes later, her entire $12,145 investment account had been wired away
Article Text:
Powell-Loggins continues to deny that she shared information with the callers. (Representational AI photo)

A Frantic Call And A Missing Investment

The Call May Have Distracted Her

Schwab Declines On-Camera Interview

Jazz Powell-Loggins usually does not answer calls from numbers she does not recognise. But on July 13, she decided to pick up one such call. The person on the other end claimed to be from Charles Schwab security and told her that someone was trying to sell money from her account.Powell-Loggins said the caller was speaking loudly and repeatedly told her that he was trying to help her. “And it was panic, panic immediately,” she told ABC7. She said she struggled to understand what was happening as the caller kept getting louder.About two minutes into the call, Powell-Loggins interrupted the conversation because she had to answer a call from her doctor. Soon after, an alert appeared on her phone saying that a wire transfer had been completed. The entire amount in her investment account, $12,145, was gone.The loss was devastating for Powell-Loggins, who said she had been saving the money with a specific goal in mind. “That was devastating for me,” she said. “Because my job was to make sure that my son got out of college with no debt and to help him, fulfill his dreams.”Powell-Loggins said the money was especially important because her family was already facing financial pressure.She said that her husband is battling cancer and that medical bills are increasing. She is also on disability after suffering an injury while working at a big-box warehouse store.After discovering that the money had been transferred, Powell-Loggins appealed to Charles Schwab. Five weeks later, she received a letter from the company.The letter said Schwab’s security guarantee “covers losses from unauthorized activity in your accounts”. However, the company said its investigation found that Powell-Loggins had provided a verification code to a third party, allowing the wire transfer to be completed.Powell-Loggins strongly disputed that finding. “But you guys are blaming me for an incident that I clearly told you I had nothing to do with,” she said.She also insisted that she had not given the scammers any information during the call. The case raised questions about how scammers could have obtained information that might have helped them target her account.Security experts said that information such as bank account details, routing numbers and even PIN numbers can be available for purchase on underground marketplaces known as the “dark web”.Jasika Bawa, Project Lead for Google’s Chrome Security, said short PINs can also create security risks. “I would just say, many pins are very short, like four digits. It can even be brute-forced by an attacker,” Bawa said.She explained that brute-forcing means repeatedly trying possible PIN combinations until one works. According to Bawa, scammers in Powell-Loggins’ case may have been using the frantic phone call to divert her attention while activity was taking place in her account.Bawa said banks can send alerts when money is moved. However, a person who is already dealing with a stressful and confusing phone call may fail to notice those messages.“There might be informational alerts from the bank that would say, 'Hey, by the way, like, you know, $1,000 was just moved from this place to another,'” Bawa said. “But while you're on the phone, you know, being bombarded with this, like, stressful information from the attacker, you might miss that kind of information.”ABC7 contacted Charles Schwab about the case. The company declined to provide anyone for an on-camera interview but issued a statement.“We sympathize with Ms. Powell-Loggins, whose experience is an unfortunate example of growing imposter fraud,” the company said. Schwab advised clients to be cautious, remain vigilant and protect their personal information.The company did not answer follow-up questions. The questions included what Schwab could have done to prevent the incident, whether a withdrawal involving an account’s entire balance should trigger additional scrutiny, and what evidence the company had that Powell-Loggins provided a verification code to the scammers.Powell-Loggins continues to deny that she shared information with the callers. “I've shown nothing but integrity and hung out with this company. And for them to tell me, we believe you have something to do with it. We're not giving you back a dime. Good riddance. That was devastating to me,” she said.She has decided to continue pursuing the matter. Powell-Loggins is taking her case to arbitration and has contacted local police and the FBI.
Article Summary: Jazz Powell-Loggins received a frantic call from someone claiming to be from Charles Schwab security. She interrupted the call because she had to answer a call from her doctor. Soon after, an alert appeared on her phone saying that a wire transfer had been completed. The entire amount in her investment account, $12,145, was gone.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: Dire straits: Brand on the run as Trump suggests Hormuz can be renamed in his honor
Article Text:
Trump’s latest push to rename the Strait of Hormuz adds another chapter to his growing campaign of political branding and geographic renaming

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Donald Trump has rescued a canal, invaded a country, conquered a gulf, annexed a lake -- at least on American maps -- and put his name on a performing-arts center. He now appears to have set his sights on the hottest waterway on the planet.The MAGA boss suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” -- because if you cannot solve a problem, you can at least rename it.The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for US federal purposes. Last week he signed an executive order changing Lake Ontario to Lake America, saying the US had been treated badly by Canada. He then helpfully suggested that the Atlantic or Pacific could be next, saying, “We have a gulf and we have a lake…Now all we need is an ocean. ”The President, someone jibed, appears to be collecting bodies of water like refrigerator magnets.The joke became even better when Google Maps and Apple Maps fell in line.Google changed Lake Ontario to Lake America for US users over the weekend. Apple followed on Tuesday. Canadians, however, continue to see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere may see both names. In other words, the lake has acquired the geographic equivalent of dual citizenship.The tech companies' compliance prompted criticism from illuminati who argue that private corporations should not allow political pressure to dictate historical and geographic nomenclature. MapQuest, an internet relic many Americans had forgotten existed, refused to make the change and suddenly discovered the most effective marketing strategy in Silicon Valley: stand up to Trump. Its downloads reportedly surged, giving it the kind reception normally reserved for rock bands that haven’t toured for a long time or sports legends making a comeback.There is also an awkward business joke buried underneath all this. Trump built his political persona partly on branding himself as a master businessman, but his corporate record includes repeated failures and bankruptcies in hotels and casinos; His casino empire alone went through multiple Chapter 11 restructurings. Trump-branded ventures have also included products and licensing deals that did not last.Late-night television has naturally treated Trump's naming obsession as premium material. The Atlantic, meanwhile, took the joke to its logical conclusion in a satirical vision of a future America in which everything is renamed “America” or “Trump,” leaving citizens unable to distinguish between brands of products, goods, and structures.Political analysts however see a serious calculation behind what many consider trolling. The renaming campaign sure is presidential theater -- cheap to stage, impossible for the internet and tv to resist, and almost guaranteed to ignite social media. But it also serves to distract people from more pressing issues -- such as cost of living and democracy going down the tubes.
Article Summary: Trump suggested on his social media account on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz could be renamed the “Trump Strait” The proposal is the latest addition to what has become an extraordinary Trump-era renaming and branding binge. In January 2025, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf Of America for US federal purposes.
